strengths: Identifies and formally characterizes two concrete pathologies of the closest prior work (BayesIMP): underfitting caused by non-stationarity of the 'nuclear-dominant' kernel (Prop. 1-2) and variance collapse out-of-support caused by finite-dimensional posterior approximations. This diagnosis is rigorous and well-supported by both theory and empirical figures (Figs. 3-5).

The core methodological idea (expanding the function class via a linear-kernel GP prior on f, combined with a Mercer/spectral decomposition of the second-stage RKHS-valued conditional mean embedding) is elegant and yields closed-form posterior moments (Theorem 1) while formally recovering the SOTA point estimator of Singh et al. (2024) as the posterior mean — a nice unification of frequentist kernel estimation and Bayesian UQ.

Extensive and careful theoretical treatment: measure-theoretic justification of exchanging expectation and unbounded linear functionals (Prop. 3, using an isonormal GP formalism), full derivations of posterior mean/variance/covariance for incremental and averaged effects, and a consistency theorem for the proposed calibration procedure under bootstrap plug-in estimation.

A genuinely novel calibration algorithm that tunes the free spectral measure parameter to optimize empirical coverage, which is shown empirically to meaningfully improve calibration beyond the untuned posterior.

Empirical validation spans multiple settings (toy simulation, benchmark DAG with unobserved confounders, real-data-informed healthcare simulator) and a downstream causal Bayesian optimization task, consistently showing IMPspec outperforms or matches baselines in RMSE, calibration error, and cumulative regret, with ablations isolating the effects of calibration, sample splitting, and BayesIMP hyperparameter tuning.
weaknesses: Experiments use fairly small sample sizes (mostly n=100, one case n=500) and low-dimensional synthetic/semi-synthetic DAGs; there is no empirical evidence of scalability to larger n or higher-dimensional covariates, despite the paper mentioning minibatch SGD as a possible fix without testing it.

Baselines are limited to BayesIMP, a naive sampling GP, and one doubly-robust frequentist estimator; there is no comparison to other modern UQ approaches (e.g., conformal prediction for causal effects, other Bayesian nonparametric causal methods) that could contextualize the calibration/coverage gains more broadly.

The calibration algorithm (Algorithm 2) requires a nested loop of grid search over spectral parameters × test points × interval levels × bootstrap replications, which could be computationally expensive; the paper does not report wall-clock costs or scaling behavior of this calibration step.

The method still assumes a known causal graph/identification strategy (back-door or front-door) and characteristic, continuous, bounded kernels with computable Mercer decompositions; while this is standard in the kernel causal-inference literature, the practical sensitivity to kernel/spectral-measure choice for the K̃_V approximation (Monte Carlo with potentially large sample sizes) is only lightly explored.

The presentation is extremely dense and notation-heavy (many appendix pages of proofs), which may hinder accessibility and reproducibility checks by readers not already expert in RKHS/GP correspondence theory, and the main text relies heavily on appendix material for full understanding of key claims (e.g., the multi-dataset/causal-fusion formulas).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and previously under-examined problem: constructing valid GP-based uncertainty quantification for causal effects under continuous treatments, building on the RKHS-based estimator of Singh et al. (2024).

Strong theoretical contribution: Theorem 1 gives closed-form posterior mean/variance for the interventional causal function, and the appendix rigorously proves that the posterior mean coincides exactly with the state-of-the-art kernel ridge regression estimator, extending the L^2-convergent representation of the (possibly unbounded) linear functional construction with a full measure-theoretic proof (Proposition 3, Lemma 4).

The paper carefully diagnoses two concrete failure modes of the closest competing method (BayesIMP): non-stationarity-induced underfitting and out-of-support variance collapse. These are not just claimed but proven mathematically (Propositions 1-2 in the appendix) and then demonstrated empirically in Figs. 3-4, which is a compelling combination of theory and practice.

A novel closed-form weighted marginal-likelihood objective (WLL) is derived for hyperparameter training when direct likelihoods are intractable, and a new calibration algorithm adapting the Syring-Martin general Bayesian calibration framework to the spectral measure is introduced with a consistency proof (Theorem 6) under stated smoothness/sample-splitting conditions.

Experiments span multiple settings (toy simulation, synthetic causal DAG benchmark, and causal Bayesian optimization including a healthcare-motivated task) and consistently show IMPspec improving both point-estimate accuracy and calibration relative to BayesIMP, a sampling GP, and a doubly-robust frequentist baseline; ablations in the appendix (sample-splitting, MC-approximated BayesIMP kernel, optimizing BayesIMP's smoothing variance) strengthen the empirical claims.
The paper is unusually transparent about assumptions (Appendix A.1) and includes an extensive, largely self-contained set of proofs, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Experimental validation is fairly small-scale: sample sizes are mostly n=100 (or n=500 for one ATT task), and results are averaged over only 50 trials; in several tables (e.g., Table 2 RMSE, Table 3 front-door regret) the reported standard deviations are comparable to or larger than the differences between methods, making it hard to assess the robustness/significance of the claimed improvements.

All comparisons are against the authors' own re-implementations of a small set of baselines (BayesIMP, a sampling GP, and one doubly-robust estimator); there is no comparison to other plausible alternatives, e.g., conformal-prediction-based UQ for causal effects, or other recent Bayesian nonparametric causal inference methods, which would help contextualize the significance of the gains.

The 'application in healthcare' is not real patient-level data but a semi-synthetic simulator built from a single external linear regression fit (Carvalhal et al., 2010) combined with a separately simulated confounder-generating process; this limits the strength of the practical/real-world claim of the healthcare experiment.

The Gaussian-approximate credible interval construction (forward-KL GP projection of the true, non-Gaussian process γ) is a heuristic device whose approximation quality is not theoretically bounded; the paper relies entirely on empirical calibration checks (which are themselves only asymptotically justified and require sample splitting/bootstrap) rather than any finite-sample coverage guarantee.

Computational complexity remains O(n^3) from GP matrix inversions; while minibatching is mentioned as a possible remedy for large n, this is not demonstrated, leaving scalability to realistic dataset sizes (well beyond n=100-500) untested.

The spectral calibration procedure (Algorithm 2) restricts the spectral measure to a simple parametric family (e.g., a single Gaussian with scalar bandwidth β for continuous V), which may be too inflexible in higher dimensions or for more complex V distributions; the discrete/countable-case extensions are only sketched, not evaluated.

The probabilistic surrogate models (10)-(11) used for tractable inference are explicitly acknowledged as not being structural models (e.g., not requiring Z→V in the DAG); the practical consequences of this mismatch between the inference model and the true causal DAG are not empirically stress-tested beyond the specific simulated settings chosen by the authors.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored problem: principled Bayesian uncertainty quantification for causal effects of continuous treatments identified via RKHS-based estimators (Singh et al., 2024). This is a meaningful gap, as existing doubly-robust/frequentist approaches struggle with continuous treatments and conditional effects.

The core technical idea—expanding the function class by placing an isonormal (linear-kernel) GP prior directly on the linear functional f rather than trying to construct a bespoke GP whose sample paths lie in the RKHS, combined with a Mercer spectral decomposition to place independent scalar GP priors on the coordinate functions of the conditional mean embedding—is elegant and well-motivated. It cleanly sidesteps the known difficulty of constructing GP priors with RKHS sample paths (Lukić and Beder, 2001).

The posterior mean is shown to exactly recover the state-of-the-art kernel ridge regression estimator of Singh et al. (2024) (Theorem 1 and Section A.5), which is a nice consistency property: the method is a genuine Bayesian extension of an established, minimax-optimal estimator rather than a new competing point estimator.

Rigorous supporting mathematical treatment in the appendix: careful measure-theoretic construction of the posterior (regular conditional distributions, standard Borel space arguments), an L²-convergence proof that the model is well-defined despite f being an a.s.-unbounded functional (Proposition 3, Lemma 4), explicit derivation of posterior mean/variance/covariance formulas for γ and its incremental/average versions, and a consistency result for the calibration procedure (Theorem 6) tied to the convergence rates of Singh et al. (2024).

Clear, well-substantiated diagnosis of the weaknesses of the main competitor BayesIMP (Chau et al., 2021b): the paper proves (Propositions 1–2) that the nuclear-dominant kernel construction causes basis functions to collapse exponentially with distance from the spectral measure's mode, explaining observed underfitting, and separately shows analytically (Section A.6.2) why the finite-dimensional posterior variance approximation used by BayesIMP causes variance collapse out-of-distribution. This is much more than an empirical comparison; it gives a principled explanation for the failure modes, which are then confirmed in experiments (Fig. 3, Fig. 4).

The experimental section is reasonably comprehensive: a toy example with causal data fusion, a more complex synthetic benchmark with unobserved confounders and both back-door/front-door identification, and a downstream causal Bayesian optimization application including a healthcare-motivated simulator. IMPspec is compared against multiple relevant baselines (BayesIMP, sampling-based GP, doubly robust continuous treatment estimator, standard/causal BO) on both point-estimate accuracy (RMSE) and calibration error, both in- and out-of-distribution.

The introduction of a spectral calibration procedure (Section 5.2, adapting Syring and Martin (2019) to this causal/RKHS setting) that tunes the spectral measure to improve empirical coverage is a nice practical addition, and ablations (Table 1, Appendix C.1.4) show it meaningfully improves calibration without hurting RMSE.

The paper is transparent about limitations of its own approximations (e.g., the GP-KL projection used to get tractable credible intervals since the exact posterior of γ is not Gaussian; the reliance on Monte Carlo estimation of a matrix K̃_V; noting BayesIMP's issue could be avoided when W=∅ but generally cannot).

Extensive appendix material generalizes the framework to the causal data fusion setting (two-dataset case) and to incremental/average treatment effects, which meaningfully broadens applicability beyond the specific point estimator considered in the main text.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation, while multi-faceted, is limited to relatively low-dimensional, small-sample (n=100–500) synthetic/semi-synthetic settings; there is no evaluation on higher-dimensional or larger real-world datasets, leaving open questions about scalability given the stated O(n^3) cost of the GP machinery (mitigated only by a suggestion to use minibatch stochastic gradients, which is not empirically demonstrated).

The healthcare application is a simulator calibrated loosely to a single regression coefficient (R^2=0.13) from an external study (Carvalhal et al., 2010) rather than a genuine real-data application with ground truth, and the authors note they could not access the original BayesIMP healthcare data, which somewhat weakens the practical/'real-world' framing of this experiment.

The number of independent trials (50) for each experiment is relatively modest given the noisiness of calibration-error metrics; while bootstrap confidence bands are reported, the qualitative story (e.g., in Fig. 3/4) could benefit from a larger number of trials or additional random seeds/DGPs to establish robustness of the RMSE/calibration rankings.

The identification assumptions (Assumptions 1–3, e.g., characteristic/bounded/continuous kernels, σ-compactness, positive Mercer eigenvalues) are somewhat strong and their practical verifiability for arbitrary chosen kernels/spectral measures ν is not discussed in much depth; the impact of misspecifying ν (beyond the Gaussian spectral-measure ablation) on the quality of posterior uncertainty is not extensively explored.

The calibration algorithm (Algorithm 2) involves a nested loop over spectral parameter grid × test points × interval levels × bootstrap replications, which could become computationally expensive as the grid/test-point sets grow; no runtime or computational cost comparison to BayesIMP or standard CBO is reported, despite claims of practical inference tractability.

While the paper convincingly explains BayesIMP's failure modes theoretically and empirically, the comparison set of baselines is somewhat narrow for a 2026 submission—e.g., no comparison to more recent deep/neural conditional density or normalizing-flow-based causal uncertainty methods, nor to conformal-prediction-based approaches for continuous treatments, leaving the relative competitiveness of IMPspec against a broader modern landscape somewhat unaddressed.

The reliance on a GP-KL projection for credible intervals (Section 4.2) is only justified as being the process minimizing KL divergence to the true (non-Gaussian) posterior; no empirical or theoretical characterization of how well-calibrated this Gaussian approximation is in cases of strong non-Gaussianity (e.g., heavy-tailed γ, as illustrated in Fig. 2) is provided beyond the specific experimental calibration curves shown.

strengths: Addresses an important open problem: principled uncertainty quantification for function-valued causal estimands (CATE, dose-response, ATT), building naturally on the RKHS-representation approach of Singh et al. (2024).

The core technical idea—relaxing the RKHS constraint on f and using the Mercer spectral expansion to place standard, tractable GP priors on the vector-valued embedding mu—is a genuinely useful trick that sidesteps a known hard problem (constructing GP priors whose sample paths lie in a prescribed RKHS), and is well-motivated by concrete pathologies (nonstationarity/underfitting and finite-dimensional variance collapse) shown both theoretically and empirically for the closest competing method, BayesIMP.

Strong internal consistency: the posterior mean is proven to exactly recover the established point estimator of Singh et al. (2024), so the method can be viewed as a rigorous 'error bar' around an already validated estimator rather than a wholly new (and thus less trusted) point estimate.

Extensive and rigorous supporting theory in the appendix: convergence proofs for the interventional-process representation, full derivation of closed-form posterior moments (including for incremental/averaged effects), sensitivity analysis of posterior moments to likelihood misspecification, and a consistency proof for the calibration-loss estimator.

Thorough empirical evaluation across a toy example, a well-known synthetic benchmark DAG, causal Bayesian optimization tasks, and a real 401(k) dataset at realistic scale (n≈10,000), consistently showing improved calibration and interval scores relative to BayesIMP, sampling GPs, and frequentist baselines (ORF, continuous DR).

Commendable transparency and robustness checks: ablations on sample splitting, number of bootstrap replications, kernel choice, heavy-tailed noise, and limited treatment support; the paper even reports and corrects apparent errors found in the baseline implementation, and reports runtime/memory for practical feasibility.
weaknesses: The tractability of the method rests on a surrogate coordinate-wise Gaussian likelihood for the spectral features of V (Eq. 11), which is acknowledged to be an approximation rather than a structural assumption; while bounds on the resulting posterior approximation error are derived, they are qualitative/asymptotic and depend on an unknown mis-specification parameter epsilon, so the practical severity of this approximation is only indirectly addressed via post-hoc empirical calibration.

Core inference and calibration algorithms scale as O(n^3) (matrix inversions) and the calibration procedure requires repeated bootstrap resampling and retraining, which may be costly at larger scale; minibatch SGD is used for hyperparameter fitting but the underlying moment computations still require full-data linear algebra, and truly large-scale (sparse) extensions are left to future work.

Most synthetic experiments use small sample sizes (n=100), and the sole large real-data application (401k) has no ground truth, making it a qualitative plausibility check rather than a rigorous validation of calibration/coverage claims at scale.

The main paper is very dense and defers essentially all proofs, several important derivations (e.g., causal data-fusion setting, incremental/averaged effects), and most ablations to an extensive appendix, which somewhat limits self-containedness and may make it harder for readers to verify central claims without substantial extra effort.

Frequentist comparisons are relatively limited (Kennedy et al. 2017's doubly robust estimator adapted favorably to a fixed-covariate subproblem, and ORF, which is mismatched to the nonlinear DGP), so the empirical claim of 'remaining competitive' with frequentist debiased methods rests on a narrow set of baselines that may not represent the strongest available alternatives.

The practical calibration procedure only tunes a single scalar/simple parametric family (variance of the spectral measure), which, while shown effective in the reported experiments, may not fully correct coverage errors in more complex or higher-dimensional settings where the Gaussian moment-matching approximation is more severely violated.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine gap: GP-based uncertainty quantification for interventional (causal) functions expressed via RKHS inner products, building on Singh et al. (2024). The idea of relaxing the RKHS boundedness constraint on f and using a spectral (Mercer) representation for the vector-valued embedding mu is a clean and technically sound way to sidestep the well-known difficulty of constructing GP priors whose sample paths lie in a prescribed RKHS.

Theorem 4.1 gives fully closed-form posterior mean/variance expressions, and the authors rigorously show (Section A.5) that the posterior mean recovers exactly the kernel-ridge-regression estimator of Singh et al. (2024), which is an important and non-trivial equivalence result that ties the new Bayesian machinery to an already validated frequentist estimator.

The paper provides a thorough theoretical treatment of the competing method BayesIMP (Chau et al., 2021b), with new propositions (A.10, A.11) proving that its nuclear-dominant kernel construction is nonstationary and leads to basis-function collapse away from the measure's mode, and a separate derivation showing the finite-dimensional approximation used at inference time causes variance collapse out-of-support. This is a valuable, well-substantiated diagnostic contribution beyond the main method itself.

Extensive empirical validation across four settings (toy causal-data-fusion example, synthetic back-door benchmark against frequentist baselines like ORF and continuous DR, three causal Bayesian optimization tasks including a healthcare simulator, and a real 401(k) dataset at n≈10000 with reported runtime/memory) with consistent metrics (RMSE, calibration error, interval score) and appropriate uncertainty bars (bootstrap CIs).

Substantial appendix work on robustness: a formal error-propagation analysis of the surrogate Gaussian likelihood used for tractability (Section A.4, with chi-squared/TV bounds and explicit posterior-moment error bounds), consistency proof for the calibration-loss estimator (Theorem C.9), and various ablations (kernel choice, bootstrap replications, sample-splitting, heavy-tailed noise, limited treatment support) that probe sensitivity of the proposed method rather than just showcasing favorable settings.

The proposed calibration procedure (tuning the spectral measure via a bootstrap-based objective) is a practical and reasonably well-justified add-on that empirically improves coverage substantially in the reported experiments.
weaknesses: The real-data case study (401(k)) has no ground-truth causal effect, so it can only be assessed qualitatively for plausibility; this weakens the paper's claim of demonstrating practical utility at scale, since no calibration/coverage claims can be empirically checked there.

The core tractability relies on a surrogate coordinate-wise Gaussian noise model for the Mercer coefficients (Eq. 11), which the authors admit is 'not standard' and only exact under restrictive conditions (linear kernel, small/Gaussian conditional noise). While Section A.4 bounds the resulting posterior error via a chi-squared divergence assumption, that assumption itself (bounded second moment of the likelihood ratio) is not verified or estimated in the experiments, so it is unclear how large the real approximation error is in practice.

Computational complexity remains O(n^3) per hyperparameter/inference step (mitigated only via minibatch SGD for training, not for exact posterior inference), and scalability beyond the ~10^4-sample 401(k) example is not demonstrated; the authors acknowledge sparse approximations are left to future work, limiting the near-term applicability to larger datasets common in some high-stakes domains.

The empirical comparisons, while reasonably broad, are somewhat narrow in baseline diversity for the frequentist side (only Kennedy et al. 2017 and ORF), and the synthetic DGPs (toy, benchmark DAG) are relatively low-dimensional and smooth, so it is unclear how well the method's advantages over BayesIMP/sampling-GP would persist in higher-dimensional or more adversarial settings.

The presentation is extremely dense, with the bulk of the mathematical machinery (spectral GP construction, posterior derivations, error-propagation bounds, BayesIMP failure-mode proofs) deferred to a very long appendix (~38 pages); the main text alone leaves several technical claims (e.g., exact reproduction of the KRR estimator, calibration consistency) essentially unproven, which could make independent verification difficult without substantial extra effort.

The contribution, although technically elegant, is somewhat incremental in scope: it is essentially (i) a specific prior-construction fix for a known pathology in GP-RKHS representations combined with (ii) a bootstrap calibration wrapper, applied to an existing causal estimator (Singh et al., 2024); the conceptual novelty relative to standard GP regression and existing spectral/Mercer techniques is modest even though the causal application and the equivalence results are valuable.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: principled uncertainty quantification for function-valued causal estimands (CATEs, dose-response curves), where standard debiased/influence-function machinery breaks down due to lack of bounded Riesz representers.

The core technical idea—relaxing the RKHS constraint via a linear-kernel GP prior for f and using the Mercer/spectral expansion to place independent scalar GP priors on the coordinate functions of the conditional mean embedding μ—is elegant and yields genuinely closed-form posterior moments (Theorem 4.1), which is a nontrivial achievement given the infinite-dimensional, RKHS-valued nature of μ.

A conceptually appealing and practically important property is that the posterior mean of IMPspec is proven to exactly recover the kernel causal estimator of Singh et al. (2024) (Section A.5), so the method can be understood as principled, calibrated uncertainty quantification wrapped around an established, minimax-optimal point estimator rather than an entirely new (and possibly worse) point estimator.

Strong and convincing theoretical + empirical diagnosis of the main competing method (BayesIMP/Chau et al. 2021b): Propositions A.10/A.11 rigorously show that the nuclear-dominant kernel construction used by BayesIMP is provably nonstationary and its basis functions collapse away from the mode of the integrating measure, and Section A.6.2 shows the finite-dimensional approximation used for tractability induces posterior variance collapse out-of-support. These theoretical claims are directly corroborated in Figures 3-4 (systematic underfitting and out-of-support miscalibration for BayesIMP).

Extensive and honest supporting theoretical apparatus in the appendix: a full accounting of the posterior approximation error induced by the surrogate Gaussian likelihoods (Section A.4, with χ2/TV bounds and moment-perturbation bounds), a proof of asymptotic consistency of the calibration-loss estimator (Theorem C.9), and full derivations/proofs for the causal data-fusion setting, incremental effects, and average effects—this is unusually thorough and improves confidence in soundness.

Empirical evaluation is broad and well-designed: a controlled toy example, a well-known synthetic benchmark DAG with multiple frequentist and Bayesian baselines (ORF, continuous-treatment doubly robust, sampling GP, BayesIMP), causal Bayesian optimization tasks (front-door, back-door, and a healthcare simulator), and a real large-scale 401(k) dataset with reported runtime/memory feasibility. Reported gains in calibration error and interval score are consistent across settings, and RMSE remains competitive (not just calibration-favorable at the cost of estimation quality).

Reproducibility is well supported: detailed algorithms (Alg. 1-3) for inference, training and calibration are given, hyperparameter/training settings, kernel choices and dataset preprocessing are documented at length in the appendix, and multiple robustness ablations (heavy-tailed noise, limited treatment support, kernel family, bootstrap replications, sample-splitting) are included for the toy experiment.
weaknesses: The observation model for the spectral coordinates (Eq. 11, additive Gaussian noise on ϕ_{V,i}(V)) is a surrogate/approximate likelihood whose fidelity to the true data-generating process is unclear in general; while Section A.4 provides bounds on the resulting posterior approximation error, these bounds are in terms of an abstract likelihood-ratio moment condition ε that is not estimated or verified in any experiment, so it is hard to assess how tight or informative this analysis is in practice.

The main direct competitor baseline for the core uncertainty-quantification comparison is essentially BayesIMP (plus a sampling GP and, in the synthetic benchmark, ORF/continuous DR); given how convincingly the paper demonstrates BayesIMP's pathologies, a reader may wonder whether the empirical margin would be as large against a more carefully tuned or alternative Bayesian causal UQ baseline (e.g., non-GP Bayesian nonparametric approaches, or conformal-style calibration wrappers for the same point estimator).

Computational scalability remains a concern for large n despite the minibatch training trick: posterior inference/calibration still requires O(n^3) dense kernel matrix operations (the calibration bootstrap in particular re-runs training/inference many times), and the 401(k) case study (n ≈ 9915) required a dedicated GPU with ~16GB memory and non-trivial runtime, raising questions about applicability to substantially larger real-world datasets without further sparsification.

The spectral-measure calibration procedure (Section 5.2) is restricted to a simple parametric family (e.g., isotropic Gaussian centered at the empirical mean, with a scalar bandwidth grid-searched over a handful of values), which may be too limited to correct calibration in more complex or heteroskedastic settings; the paper's own toy-example ablation shows this family only partially resolves miscalibration relative to well-specified alternatives.

The 401(k) real-data application has no ground-truth causal effect, so it functions only as a qualitative plausibility/feasibility check rather than a genuine validation of the method's uncertainty estimates at scale; the reported positive CATE trend is consistent with prior literature but cannot itself corroborate calibration or interval validity.

The technical construction, while carefully executed, combines fairly standard ingredients (Mercer/spectral expansion of RKHS elements, GP regression posterior equivalence to KRR, moment-matched Gaussian posterior approximation) in a way that is elegant but incremental relative to Singh et al. (2024) and the existing GP/RKHS equivalence literature (e.g., Kanagawa et al. 2018); the conceptual novelty is more in the careful engineering and diagnosis of prior pitfalls than in fundamentally new machinery.
